items.title: Ideal linear Penning mode-frequency invariant
items.design_state: Complete conditional trace proof; reader state-solution clarification retained and manifest synchronized at Step 3a. Actual draft def-qft-example-data convention inspected; independent supplier acceptance is not asserted.
items.statement:
Let $q
e0$ be a signed charge in coulombs, $M>0$ a rest-mass energy in joules, $c>0$ the speed of light in metres per second, and $\mathbf B\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ a constant magnetic-field vector in teslas. Set $m:=M/c^2>0$. Let $K\in\mathbb R^{3	imes3}$ be a real symmetric matrix with $\operatorname{tr}K=0$, with units volts per square metre, and define the quadratic scalar potential $\Phi(\mathbf r):=	frac12\mathbf r^{T}K\mathbf r$ for $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres. Thus $\partial_i\partial_j\Phi=K_{ij}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i^2\Phi=\operatorname{tr}K=0$. Put $\alpha:=qc^2/M=q/m$, $D:=-\alpha K$, and define $C:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ by $C\mathbf w:=\alpha\,\mathbf w	imes\mathbf B$. The ideal linear model is the real linear map $A:\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R^3$, $A(\mathbf r,\mathbf v):=(\mathbf v,D\mathbf r+C\mathbf v)$, equivalently $A= egin{pmatrix}0&I_3\D&C\end{pmatrix}$. Equivalently, its equations are $\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf v$ and $\dot{\mathbf v}=-(qc^2/M)K\mathbf r+(qc^2/M)\mathbf v	imes\mathbf B$. The entries of $\mathbf r,\mathbf v$ are their real numerical coordinates in the fixed SI units. A state solution on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^1$ map $y=(\mathbf r,\mathbf v):I	o\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the displayed equations for every $t\in I$. Here $\mathbf v$ has units metres per second, $D$ has units inverse seconds squared, and $C$ has units inverse seconds.

Define a linear mode to be a complex eigenvector of the complexified state matrix $A$; its eigenvalue $+i\omega$ or $-i\omega$ gives the time factor $e^{\pm i\omega t}$, with angular frequency $\omega>0$ in radians per second. Assume the complexification of $A$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $+i\omega_1,-i\omega_1,+i\omega_2,-i\omega_2,+i\omega_3,-i\omega_3$, where each $\omega_j$ is counted with its eigenvalue multiplicity. Define the free cyclotron angular frequency $\omega_c:=|q|c^2|\mathbf B|/M$. Then

$$\omega_c^2=\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2+\omega_3^2.$$

Consequently, if $
u_c:=\omega_c/(2\pi)$ and $
u_j:=\omega_j/(2\pi)$ are the corresponding ordinary frequencies in hertz, then $
u_c^2=
u_1^2+
u_2^2+
u_3^2$. The claim is conditional on the stated uniform-field, harmonic-quadrupole, and complete stable-mode hypotheses; it is an identity for this linear model.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], the inertial-mass coefficient in the SI equation is $q/m=qc^2/M=\alpha$. Block multiplication gives $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}D&C\\CD&D+C^2\end{pmatrix}$, so $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=2\operatorname{tr}D+\operatorname{tr}(C^2)$. [L1, A1, algebra]

1.2 By [A2], write the complexification as $A=P\Lambda P^{-1}$, where $\Lambda$ is diagonal with the six stated eigenvalues. Then $A^2=P\Lambda^2P^{-1}$; the finite-sum identity $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\sum_{k,\ell}X_{k\ell}Y_{\ell k}=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^2)=\sum_{j=1}^3((i\omega_j)^2+(-i\omega_j)^2)=-2\sum_{j=1}^3\omega_j^2$. [A2, algebra]

2.1 Since $D=-\alpha K$ and $\operatorname{tr}K=0$, $\operatorname{tr}D=0$. In the fixed right-handed Cartesian coordinates, $C$ has matrix $\alpha\begin{pmatrix}0&B_3&-B_2\\-B_3&0&B_1\\B_2&-B_1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so the diagonal entries of $C^2$ are $-\alpha^2(B_2^2+B_3^2)$, $-\alpha^2(B_1^2+B_3^2)$, and $-\alpha^2(B_1^2+B_2^2)$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(C^2)=-2\alpha^2|\mathbf B|^2=-2\omega_c^2$ and $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=-2\omega_c^2$ by step 1.1. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Equating the trace calculations in steps 2.1 and 1.2 and dividing by $-2$ gives $\omega_c^2=\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2+\omega_3^2$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 Dividing the angular-frequency identity in step 3.1 by $(2\pi)^2$ gives the same sum-of-squares identity for $\nu_c,\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3$. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: L. S. Brown and G. Gabrielse, Geonium theory: Physics of a single electron or ion in a Penning trap, Reviews of Modern Physics 58 (1986), §II.A and §II.D, Eqs. (2.1)–(2.17), (2.70)–(2.79)
Manuel Vogel, Particle Confinement in Penning Traps: An Introduction, Springer Series on Atomic, Optical, and Plasma Physics 100 (2018), Chapter 5, §§5.1–5.3.2, Eqs. (5.1)–(5.27)
David Tong, Quantum Field Theory, Cambridge Part III complete lecture notes, §0.1 Units and Scales
X. Fan et al., Measurement of the Electron Magnetic Moment, Physical Review Letters 130, 071801 (2023), arXiv:2209.13084v2 (2022)

items.title: Deterministic ratio error and Taylor remainder
items.design_state: Complete local algebraic proof; no in-run supplier.
items.statement:
Define $R:\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ by $R(a,c):=1+a/c$. Here $c$ is only the positive denominator variable in this lemma, not the speed of light. For real $\delta a,\delta c$ and nonnegative bounds $\epsilon_a,\epsilon_c$ satisfying $|\delta a|\le\epsilon_a$ and $|\delta c|\le\epsilon_c<c$, both denominators are positive and

$$\left|R(a+\delta a,c+\delta c)-R(a,c)\right|\le\frac{c\epsilon_a+|a|\epsilon_c}{c(c-\epsilon_c)}.$$

For the first-order statement, write $x=(a,c)$, $h=(u,v)$, and $\|h\|_2:=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$. Suppose the segment $\{x+th:0\le t\le1\}$ lies in the closed rectangle $Q=[A_-,A_+]\times[c_-,c_+]$, where $A_-\le A_+$ and $0<c_-\le c_+$. Define $A_*:=\max(|A_-|,|A_+|)$, $K_Q:=(A_*+c_+/2)/c_-^3$, and the real-linear map $L_x(u,v):=u/c-av/c^2$. The total derivative of $R$ at $x$ means a real-linear map $L$ such that $\lim_{h\to0}|R(x+h)-R(x)-L(h)|/\|h\|_2=0$. Then $L_x$ is the total derivative, and

$$\left|R(x+h)-R(x)-L_x(h)\right|\le K_Q\|h\|_2^2.$$
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 From [A1], $c+\delta c\ge c-\epsilon_c>0$. Thus both ratio values are defined, and subtracting their fractions gives
$R(a+\delta a,c+\delta c)-R(a,c)=\frac{c\delta a-a\delta c}{c(c+\delta c)}$. [A1, algebra]

1.2 For $\eta\to0$ with $c+\eta>0$, the coordinate difference quotients are
$\frac{R(a+\eta,c)-R(a,c)}{\eta}=\frac1c$ and
$\frac{R(a,c+\eta)-R(a,c)}{\eta}=-\frac{a}{c(c+\eta)}$.
Their limits give the candidate linear map $L_x(u,v)=u/c-av/c^2$; the total-derivative conclusion follows from the full remainder estimate below. [A2, algebra]

1.3 Direct subtraction gives
$R(x+h)-R(x)-L_x(h)=\frac{av^2-cuv}{c^2(c+v)}$. [A2, algebra]

2.1 The triangle inequality gives $|c\delta a-a\delta c|\le c\epsilon_a+|a|\epsilon_c$, while [A1] gives $c(c+\delta c)\ge c(c-\epsilon_c)>0$. Dividing these positive-denominator bounds proves the displayed deterministic ratio-error inequality. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since the segment lies in $Q$, $c,c+v\ge c_-$, $c\le c_+$, and $|a|\le A_*$. Also $2|uv|\le u^2+v^2$, because $(|u|-|v|)^2\ge0$. Therefore
$|av^2-cuv|\le A_*v^2+c_+|uv|\le(A_*+c_+/2)(u^2+v^2)$, and $c^2(c+v)\ge c_-^3$. Combining these estimates with the exact remainder in step 1.3 gives
$|R(x+h)-R(x)-L_x(h)|\le K_Q\|h\|_2^2$. [A2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 For fixed $x=(a,c)$ with $c>0$, choose $Q=[a-1,a+1]\times[c/2,3c/2]$, so $x$ is interior and its lower second-coordinate bound is positive. For every sufficiently small $h$, both endpoints lie in $Q$, and convexity places the segment there. Step 2.2 then gives
$\frac{|R(x+h)-R(x)-L_x(h)|}{\|h\|_2}\le K_Q\|h\|_2\to0$.
By the stated definition, $DR(x)=L_x$. [A2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Hypothetical calibration error interval
items.design_state: Complete conditional numerical verification with stipulated interval values; no empirical data are used.
items.statement: Take the stipulated nominal values $a=1\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $c=100\,\mathrm{Hz}$, and interval bounds $\epsilon_a=0.1\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $\epsilon_c=1\,\mathrm{Hz}$. The nominal ratio $R=1+a/c$ is dimensionless, and the exact absolute error bound is $11/9900$. These inputs are hypothetical interval values: they are not measurements, error bars, a standard error, or a confidence interval, and no reported Fan et al. data are used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply [F1] using [A1]. The numerator is $100\,\mathrm{Hz}\cdot0.1\,\mathrm{Hz}+1\,\mathrm{Hz}\cdot1\,\mathrm{Hz}=11\,\mathrm{Hz}^2$, and the denominator is $100\,\mathrm{Hz}\cdot99\,\mathrm{Hz}=9900\,\mathrm{Hz}^2$. Thus every allowed perturbation has $|R(a+\delta a,c+\delta c)-R(a,c)|\le11/9900$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 The nominal value is $R(a,c)=1+1/100=101/100=1.01$; both the ratio and its bound are dimensionless because the frequency units cancel. The bound is a deterministic calculation for the stated intervals only, with no empirical or statistical interpretation. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
